paragraphs: “It is not only the pile of facts that threatens my client with ruin, gentlemen of the jury,” he began. “What really damns my client is one fact—the dead body of his father. Had this been an ordinary murder, you would have thrown out the charge, given how trivial, incomplete and fantastic the evidence is when you look at each piece separately. Or at least you would have hesitated to ruin a man’s life merely because of the prejudice against him, which he has, alas, only too well earned. But this is not an ordinary murder. This is parricide. That weighs on men’s minds, and so heavily that the very triviality and incompleteness of the evidence seems less trivial and less incomplete, even to an unprejudiced mind. How can such a prisoner be acquitted? What if he did commit the murder and goes unpunished? That is what everyone feels in his heart, almost without meaning to, by instinct.

“Yes, it is a fearful thing to shed a father’s blood—the father who gave me life, who loved me, who spared nothing for me, who grieved over my illnesses from childhood on, who worried all his life about my happiness and lived in my joys and my successes. To murder such a father—that is inconceivable. Gentlemen of the jury, what is a father—a real father? What does that great word mean? What is the great idea in that name? We have just indicated in part what a true father is and what he ought to be. In the case that so occupies us now, and over which our hearts ache—in the present case, the father, Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, did not match that idea of a father which we have just described. That is the misfortune. And indeed some fathers are a misfortune. Let us look at this misfortune a little more closely. We must shrink from nothing, gentlemen of the jury, considering how important your decision is. It is our particular duty not to shrink from any idea, like children or frightened women, as the talented prosecutor happily put it.

“But in the course of his heated speech my esteemed opponent (and he was my opponent before I had opened my mouth) exclaimed several times, ‘Oh, I will not yield the defense of the prisoner to the lawyer who has come down from Petersburg. I accuse, but I defend also!’ He exclaimed that several times, but he forgot to mention something. This terrible prisoner was grateful for twenty-three years for a mere pound of nuts, given him by the only man who had been kind to him as a child in his father’s house. Might not such a man well have remembered, for twenty-three years, how he ran about his father’s backyard ‘without boots on his feet and with his little trousers hanging by one button’—to use the words of the kind-hearted doctor, Herzenstube?

“Oh, gentlemen of the jury, why should we look more closely at this misfortune? Why repeat what we all know already? What did my client find when he arrived here, at his father’s house? And why paint my client as a heartless egoist and a monster? He is uncontrolled, he is wild and unruly—we are trying him for that now—but who is responsible for his life? Who is responsible for his having had such an improper upbringing, in spite of his excellent disposition and his grateful, sensitive heart? Did anyone train him to be reasonable? Was he enlightened by study? Did anyone love him even a little in his childhood? My client was left to the care of Providence like a beast of the field. Perhaps he thirsted to see his father after long years apart. A thousand times, perhaps, as he remembered his childhood, he may have driven away the loathsome phantoms that haunted his childish dreams, and with all his heart he may have longed to embrace his father and forgive him! And what was waiting for him? Cynical taunts, suspicions, and wrangling over money. He heard nothing but revolting talk and vicious precepts, delivered every day over the brandy. And at last he saw his father stealing his mistress from him, using his own money. Oh, gentlemen of the jury, that was cruel and revolting! And that old man was forever complaining of his son’s disrespect and cruelty. He slandered him in society, did him harm, defamed him, and bought up his unpaid debts to have him thrown into prison.

“Gentlemen of the jury, people like my client, who are fierce, unruly and uncontrolled on the surface, are sometimes—in fact most often—exceedingly tender-hearted. They simply do not show it. Do not laugh, do not laugh at my idea! The talented prosecutor laughed mercilessly just now at my client for loving Schiller—for loving the sublime and the beautiful! I would not have laughed at that, in his place. Yes, such natures—oh, let me speak in defense of such natures, so often and so cruelly misunderstood—such natures often thirst for tenderness, goodness and justice, as if in contrast to themselves, to their unruliness and ferocity. They thirst for it without knowing it. Passionate and fierce on the surface, they are painfully capable of loving a woman, for instance, with a spiritual and elevated love. Again, do not laugh at me; this is very often the case with such natures. But they cannot hide their passions, sometimes very coarse ones, and those are conspicuous and get noticed, while the inner man goes unseen. Their passions are quickly spent. But beside a noble and lofty creature, that seemingly coarse and rough man looks for a new life. He tries to correct himself, to be better, to become noble and honorable, ‘sublime and beautiful,’ however much the expression has been ridiculed.

“I said just now that I would not venture to touch on my client’s engagement. But I may say half a word. What we heard just now was not evidence. It was only the scream of a frenzied, vengeful woman. And it was not for her—oh, not for her!—to reproach him with treachery, for she has betrayed him! If she had had a little time to reflect, she would not have given such evidence. Oh, do not believe her! No, my client is not a monster, as she called him!

“The Lover of Mankind, on the eve of His Crucifixion, said: ‘I am the Good Shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep, so that not one of them might be lost.’ Let not a man’s soul be lost through us!

“I asked just now what ‘father’ means, and I exclaimed that it was a great word, a precious name. But one must use words honestly, gentlemen, and I venture to call things by their right names. A father like old Karamazov cannot be called a father and does not deserve to be. Filial love for an unworthy father is an absurdity, an impossibility. Love cannot be made out of nothing; only God can make something out of nothing.

“‘Fathers, provoke not your children to wrath,’ writes the apostle, from a heart glowing with love. It is not for my client’s sake that I quote these sacred words; I mention them for all fathers. Who has authorized me to preach to fathers? No one. But as a man and a citizen I make my appeal—_vivos voco!_ We are not long on earth. We do many evil deeds and say many evil words. So let us all seize a favorable moment, when we are gathered together, to say a good word to one another. That is what I am doing. While I am in this place, I am using my opportunity. Not for nothing has the highest authority given us this tribune—all Russia hears us! I am not speaking only for the fathers here present. I cry aloud to all fathers: ‘Fathers, provoke not your children to wrath.’ Yes, let us first fulfill Christ’s command ourselves, and only then venture to expect it of our children. Otherwise we are not fathers but enemies of our children, and they are not our children but our enemies, and we have made them our enemies ourselves. ‘What measure ye mete it shall be measured unto you again’—it is not I who say that, it is the Gospel precept: measure to others as they measure to you. How can we blame children if they measure us by our own measure?

“Not long ago a servant girl in Finland was suspected of having secretly given birth to a child. She was watched, and in the corner of the loft, behind some bricks, a box was found that no one knew anything about. It was opened, and inside was the body of a newborn child that she had killed. In the same box were the skeletons of two other babies, which, by her own confession, she had killed the moment they were born.

“Gentlemen of the jury, was she a mother to her children? She gave birth to them, indeed. But was she a mother to them? Would anyone venture to give her the sacred name of mother? Let us be bold, gentlemen, let us even be audacious. It is our duty to be so at this moment, and not to be afraid of certain words and ideas, like the Moscow women in Ostrovsky’s play, who are scared at the sound of certain words. No, let us prove that the progress of the last few years has touched even us, and let us say plainly: the father is not merely he who begets the child, but he who begets it and does his duty by it.

“Oh, of course, there is the other meaning, the other interpretation of the word ‘father,’ which insists that any father, even if he is a monster, even if he is the enemy of his children, still remains my father simply because he begot me. But this is, so to say, the mystical meaning. I cannot grasp it with my intellect; I can only accept it by faith, or, better to say, _on faith_, like many other things that I do not understand but which religion bids me believe. In that case, let it be kept outside the sphere of actual life. In the sphere of actual life, which has its own rights indeed but also lays great duties and obligations on us, in that sphere, if we want to be humane—Christian, in fact—we must, or ought to, act only on convictions justified by reason and experience, which have been put through the crucible of analysis. In a word, we must act rationally, and not as if in a dream or a delirium, so that we do no harm, so that we do not ill-treat and ruin a man. Then it will be real Christian work, not only mystical but rational and philanthropic....”
